questions.q: What kind of course is Engineering 507 B?
options: A Brief Foundations mathematics course in Anderson Engineering: an overview and six lectures, about an hour
An optional elective outside the Foundations
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.1: Paragraph 0.1 gives the format.
A is wrong: A Brief course is a first hour.
C is wrong: It is a Foundations course.
D is wrong: It is a lecture course.

questions.q: What is the backbone of this course?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 0.9: The overview credits Professors Mattuck and Miller and colleagues.
A is wrong: That backs Linear Algebra.
C is wrong: That backs Probability and Statistics.
D is wrong: That backs Physics Two.

questions.q: Why does y = C e^(kt) solve y′ = k y for any constant C?
options: Its derivative is k C e^(kt), which equals k y
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.2: One equation has a whole family of solutions.
A is wrong: C is arbitrary.
B is wrong: Its derivative is kCe^(kt).
C is wrong: It varies with t.

questions.q: What is the solution of y′ = k y with y(0) = y₀?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.3: The initial condition fixes the constant C = y₀.
B is wrong: That solves y′ = k, not y′ = ky.
C is wrong: The constant multiplies the exponential.
D is wrong: The sign of the exponent is that of k.

questions.q: Why can two solution curves of a well-behaved first-order equation never cross?
options: Because all solutions are straight lines
A crossing point would be an initial condition with two different solutions, contradicting uniqueness
Because the equation has no solutions
Because direction fields are always horizontal
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.4: Solution curves fill the plane like grain in wood.
A is wrong: Solutions need not be straight.
C is wrong: Solutions exist by the existence theorem.
D is wrong: Slopes vary from point to point.

questions.q: What is an isocline?
options: A curve along which the slope of the direction field is constant
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.6: For y′ = t − y, the isocline for slope m is the line t − y = m.
B is wrong: Solution curves are tangent to the field.
C is wrong: Equilibria have zero slope for autonomous equations.
D is wrong: It is about slopes.

questions.q: What is an autonomous first-order equation?
options: One that depends only on t
One of the form y′ = f(y), whose rule does not change with time
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.7: Equilibria are the zeros of f.
A is wrong: Autonomous equations have solutions.
B is wrong: That is y′ = f(t).
D is wrong: Linearity is a different property.

questions.q: For the logistic equation y′ = r y (1 − y/K), which equilibrium is stable?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.8: Nearby solutions move toward K; y = 0 is unstable.
A is wrong: Small populations grow away from zero.
B is wrong: K attracts nearby solutions.
C is wrong: K/2 is where growth is fastest, not an equilibrium.

questions.q: What is the general solution of y′ = t y?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.10: Separating gives dy/y = t dt, so ln|y| = t²/2 + c.
B is wrong: That solves y′ = y.
C is wrong: That solves y′ = t.
D is wrong: Substitution does not check.

questions.q: How does a tank drain by Torricelli's law, h′ = −c√h?
options: √h decreases linearly, so the tank empties in a finite time
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.11: Unlike exponential decay, it reaches zero.
A is wrong: That would be h′ = −ch.
B is wrong: The rate depends on √h.
C is wrong: It empties completely.

questions.q: If Euler's method's step size is halved, roughly what happens to the total error over a fixed interval?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 1.13: Euler's method is first order: error is proportional to h.
A is wrong: That would be a second-order method.
C is wrong: Smaller steps reduce error.
D is wrong: Error depends on step size.

questions.q: What is the integrating factor for y′ + p(t) y = q(t)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.2: Multiplying by u makes the left side the derivative of u y.
A is wrong: The factor uses p, not q.
B is wrong: That does not produce an exact derivative.
D is wrong: The factor is an exponential of the integral of p.

questions.q: What is the half-life of decay with rate constant k?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.4: Solving e^(−kt) = 1/2 gives t = ln 2/k.
A is wrong: Half-life involves ln 2.
B is wrong: Half-life has units of time.
C is wrong: That is the time constant, after which about 37 per cent remains.

questions.q: What is the solution of Newton's law of cooling, T′ = −k(T − Tₐ)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.5: The temperature approaches its surroundings exponentially.
B is wrong: The body approaches Tₐ, not zero.
C is wrong: The approach is exponential.
D is wrong: That grows rather than settles.

questions.q: In the mixing problem, what does x′ = r c − r x/V express?
options: That salt is conserved with no inflow
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.6: Brine enters at concentration c and the mixture leaves at concentration x/V.
A is wrong: The unknown is salt mass.
B is wrong: The equation is linear with a decaying transient.
C is wrong: There is an inflow term rc.

questions.q: For an RC circuit switched onto a battery, what fraction of the final voltage does the capacitor reach after one time constant RC?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.7: V = V_s(1 − e^(−t/RC)) and 1 − e^(−1) ≈ 0.63.
B is wrong: That is what remains to go.
C is wrong: It approaches the final value exponentially.
D is wrong: That is reached at about 0.69 RC.

questions.q: What are the two parts of the solution of a stable constant-coefficient linear equation?
options: A transient that dies away and a steady-state response set by the input
A growing part and a constant
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.8: Engineers often care most about the steady state.
B is wrong: They have different roles.
C is wrong: The transient decays.
D is wrong: The input also matters.

questions.q: What does superposition say about a linear equation?
options: The response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the responses
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.9: Constant multiples scale the same way.
A is wrong: They add.
C is wrong: Any combination works.
D is wrong: It is special to linear equations.

questions.q: What is Euler's formula?
options: e^(iθ) = i cos θ + sin θ
e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.11: It follows from comparing Taylor series.
A is wrong: The sine term is multiplied by i.
B is wrong: The exponent is iθ.
C is wrong: The i belongs with sine.

questions.q: For y′ + k y = cos ωt, what is the steady-state amplitude?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 2.13: The complex amplitude is 1/(k + iω), whose modulus is 1/√(k² + ω²).
A is wrong: The modulus combines k and ω in quadrature.
C is wrong: That holds only when ω = 0.
D is wrong: That is the reciprocal of the answer.

questions.q: What is the characteristic equation of m x″ + b x′ + k x = 0?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.3: Substituting e^(rt) gives (m r² + b r + k) e^(rt) = 0.
B is wrong: Each derivative contributes a power of r.
C is wrong: The coefficients stay as m, b, k.
D is wrong: Signs are preserved.

questions.q: What happens when b² − 4mk > 0?
options: The system is overdamped: it returns without oscillating
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.5: Two negative real roots give a sum of decaying exponentials.
A is wrong: That is underdamped.
B is wrong: That is undamped.
D is wrong: Both roots are negative.

questions.q: What is the general solution in the critically damped case with repeated root r?
options: c₁ cos rt + c₂ sin rt
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.6: A second solution is t e^(rt).
A is wrong: That is only one independent solution.
C is wrong: That is for imaginary roots.
D is wrong: That needs distinct roots.

questions.q: What is the natural frequency of an undamped spring-mass system?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.8: The roots of m r² + k = 0 are ±iω₀.
A is wrong: The ratio is inverted.
B is wrong: A square root is needed.
D is wrong: That mixes frequency units.

questions.q: How is a cos ωt + b sin ωt written in amplitude-phase form?
options: A sin(ωt) with A = a b
A cos(ωt) with A = a − b
A cos(ωt − φ), with A = √(a² + b²) and tan φ = b/a
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.9: The form shows the size and timing of the oscillation directly.
A is wrong: The amplitude combines a and b in quadrature.
B is wrong: The amplitude is not a product.
C is wrong: The phase shift is needed.

questions.q: What damping ratio ζ gives critical damping?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.10: ζ = b/(2√(mk)); ζ < 1 is underdamped and ζ > 1 overdamped.
A is wrong: That is undamped.
B is wrong: That is underdamped, typical of car suspensions.
D is wrong: That is overdamped.

questions.q: In the RLC analogy with a spring-mass system, what plays the role of mass?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.11: Resistance plays damping and 1/C plays the spring constant.
A is wrong: R plays damping.
B is wrong: 1/C plays stiffness.
C is wrong: q plays displacement.

questions.q: For small swings, what is the period of a pendulum of length L?
options: It grows with amplitude for small swings
questions.explain:
Paragraph 3.12: This made pendulum clocks accurate.
A is wrong: The ratio is inverted.
B is wrong: For small swings it does not depend on amplitude.
D is wrong: A square root and 2π are needed.

questions.q: By the exponential response formula, what particular solution does p(D)x = e^(at) have when p(a) ≠ 0?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.2: Since p(D)e^(at) = p(a)e^(at), dividing by p(a) gives the response.
A is wrong: One divides by p(a).
C is wrong: That works only if p(a) = 1.
D is wrong: That is for the resonant case p(a) = 0.

questions.q: For a lightly damped system, about what is the peak gain at resonance?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.5: So a damping ratio of 0.05 gives a gain of about ten.
A is wrong: Lighter damping gives a higher peak.
B is wrong: Gain near one is the low-frequency limit.
C is wrong: Only zero damping gives unbounded resonance.

questions.q: What happens to an undamped oscillator driven exactly at its natural frequency?
options: It settles to a constant amplitude
The response grows without bound, like t sin ω₀t
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.6: The exponential response formula fails, and a resonant solution growing linearly in t appears.
A is wrong: That needs damping.
B is wrong: Driving adds energy.
D is wrong: It responds at the driving frequency.

questions.q: What mainly caused the 1940 Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse, according to the lecture?
options: Simple resonance at a fixed driving frequency
Aeroelastic flutter, a self-excited instability fed by the wind
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.8: It is often wrongly described as simple resonance from a periodic push.
A is wrong: That is a different story.
B is wrong: Wind, not an earthquake.
C is wrong: The lecture distinguishes flutter from that.

questions.q: At resonance, by how much does the response lag the driving force?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.9: That is the phase at which the force does the most work.
B is wrong: That is at low frequencies.
C is wrong: That is approached at high frequencies.
D is wrong: The lag at resonance is 90°.

questions.q: How are the Fourier coefficients a_n of a 2π-periodic f found?
options: a_n = (1/π) ∫ f(t) cos nt dt over one period
a_n = ∫ f(t) dt for every n
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.11: Orthogonality of sines and cosines isolates each coefficient.
A is wrong: Coefficients are integrals.
B is wrong: That is not a coefficient.
D is wrong: Each n needs its own cosine.

questions.q: Which terms appear in the Fourier series of the standard ±1 square wave?
options: Only odd sine terms: (4/π)(sin t + sin 3t/3 + sin 5t/5 + …)
questions.explain:
Paragraph 4.12: The square wave is odd, with odd harmonics only.
A is wrong: The odd square wave has sine terms.
C is wrong: Even harmonics vanish and amplitudes fall as 1/n.
D is wrong: Infinitely many terms are needed.

questions.q: What is the Laplace transform of e^(at)?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.2: The integral of e^(−st)e^(at) from 0 to ∞ is 1/(s − a) for s > a.
A is wrong: That is the transform of e^(−at).
B is wrong: That is the transform of the constant a.
D is wrong: That is the transform of 1.

questions.q: What is the Laplace transform of f′?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.3: Integration by parts turns differentiation into multiplication by s.
A is wrong: That corresponds to integration.
C is wrong: The initial value term is missing.
D is wrong: That corresponds to multiplying by −t.

questions.q: Using the Laplace transform, what solves y′ + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 3?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.4: Y = 3/(s + 2), whose inverse is 3e^(−2t).
A is wrong: The pole is at s = −2.
B is wrong: The roles of 2 and 3 are swapped.
C is wrong: The solution is exponential.

questions.q: What is the inverse Laplace transform of 1/(s(s + 1))?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.5: Partial fractions give 1/s − 1/(s + 1).
B is wrong: The 1/s term is missing.
C is wrong: The sign is wrong.
D is wrong: That is the inverse of 1/(s + 1)².

questions.q: What is the transfer function of p(D)x = f with zero initial conditions?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.6: X = F/p(s), so W depends only on the system.
A is wrong: It is the reciprocal.
C is wrong: F depends on the input.
D is wrong: W depends on p.

questions.q: What do transfer-function poles in the left half-plane indicate?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.7: Poles are the characteristic roots; negative real parts mean decaying responses.
A is wrong: That is the right half-plane.
B is wrong: That is on the imaginary axis.
D is wrong: Poles reveal its character.

questions.q: What is the Laplace transform of a system's impulse response?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.10: The transform of δ is one, so X = W × 1.
A is wrong: That is the unit step's transform.
B is wrong: The impulse response is not zero.
D is wrong: W = 1/p(s).

questions.q: For a stable system with transfer function W(s), what is the final output for a unit step input?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 5.13: By the final value theorem, lim sX(s) = lim s·W(s)/s = W(0).
B is wrong: Not unless W(0) = 0.
C is wrong: The limit is s → 0.
D is wrong: Only if W(0) = 1.

questions.q: Substituting x = e^(λt) v into x′ = A x requires what?
options: A v = λ v: v is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.3: The eigenvalues are the roots of the characteristic equation of A.
B is wrong: A is a matrix, λ a number.
C is wrong: Eigenvectors are non-zero.
D is wrong: That is only for λ = 0.

questions.q: What equilibrium do real eigenvalues of opposite signs produce?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.6: Trajectories approach along one eigenvector and leave along the other.
B is wrong: That needs two negative eigenvalues.
C is wrong: That needs purely imaginary eigenvalues.
D is wrong: That needs complex eigenvalues with negative real part.

questions.q: What do complex eigenvalues with negative real part produce?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.7: Like an underdamped spring-mass system.
A is wrong: That needs a positive real part.
C is wrong: That needs zero real part.
D is wrong: A saddle needs real eigenvalues of opposite sign.

questions.q: In the Lotka-Volterra model, what does the term −b x y represent in the prey equation?
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.10: Encounters are proportional to the product x y.
A is wrong: That is +a x.
B is wrong: That is −c y in the predator equation.
D is wrong: There is no such term.

questions.q: Linearising the pendulum at the upright equilibrium gives what?
options: A saddle: an inverted pendulum falls
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.11: At the bottom, linearisation gives a centre.
A is wrong: That is at the bottom.
B is wrong: The upright position is unstable.
C is wrong: Linearisation gives a saddle.

questions.q: What is a limit cycle?
options: An isolated closed trajectory that attracts nearby trajectories, giving self-sustained oscillations
A family of closed orbits like a centre
Any trajectory of a linear system
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.12: Heartbeats and the van der Pol oscillator are examples.
B is wrong: Centres are not isolated.
C is wrong: It is a closed orbit.
D is wrong: Linear systems cannot have isolated limit cycles.

questions.q: What did Edward Lorenz find in 1963?
options: That all nonlinear systems are linear
Sensitive dependence on initial conditions on a strange attractor: chaos
questions.explain:
Paragraph 6.13: Nearby solutions diverge exponentially while staying bounded.
A is wrong: He found the opposite.
C is wrong: Sensitivity limits long-range prediction.
D is wrong: That dates from Laplace.
